newsitem.title: CANADA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-EDMONTON OILERS FOR SALE, OWNER SAYS.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-EDMONTON OILERS FOR SALE, OWNER SAYS.

text.p: The National Hockey League Edmonton Oilers, who won five Stanley Cup championships in the 1980s, are on the auction block and could be sold within the next three months, team owner Peter Pocklington said on Thursday.
Pocklington told a news conference he hoped the Oilers would remain in the Alberta capital under new ownership.
But local investors would have to match offers of about $85 million that have already been made by prospective U.S. owners, he said. He declined to name who made the offers.
"My heart is with the Oilers and always will be," said Pocklington. "But, objectively, it's time to move on."

Pocklington said he will sell both the team and management of the Coliseum where the club plays, adding that he hoped to finalise sale of the team, which lost between $4.4 million and $5.1 million this season, before the end of the summer.
"I hope I'll be remembered for bringing NHL hockey to Edmonton ... winning five Stanley Cups," Pocklington said.
But he may never live down trading national treasure Wayne Gretzky to Los Angeles in 1988, a move for which he is still loathed by many local fans.
Pocklington's announcement followed weeks of speculation that he would seek to unload the team to pay off a heavy debt load owed to a local bank.
But the Alberta entrepreneur said Thursday he wasn't being forced by the lender, Alberta Treasury Branch, to pay back the estimated $80 million.
Earlier this year, Pocklington unveiled plans to sell shares in all his Edmonton sports holdings to the public, but the offering was delayed repeatedly.

The Oilers were a major NHL force in the 1980s, winning five Stanley Cups in a span of seven years behind a core of future Hall of Famers such as Gretzky, Mark Messier and Paul Coffey -- all of whom were eventually let go by the cost-cutting owner.
Like many Canadian small-market clubs, the Oilers fell on rough times in the 1990s but managed to survive in Edmonton while ringing up annual losses.

Edmonton fans will anxiously await the outcome of the sale, hoping their club doesn't follow in the footsteps of the Quebec Nordiques and Winnipeg Jets, who headed south of the border to become the Colorado Avalanche and Phoenix Coyotes.
This year, Oilers fan support was bolstered by the team's strong play, which culminated in a surprise playoff berth and a stunning first-round upset of the Dallas Stars.
